source.title: Neural Anisotropy Directions
source.authors: Guillermo Ortiz-Jiménez; Apostolos Modas; Seyed-Mohsen Moosavi-Dezfooli; P. Frossard

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present
record.tranche_reason: Reports training error on CIFAR-10 representations, bearing on V1, using a study of architectural inductive bias rather than a direct reproduction of the cited claim.
record.gate_note: Other training-loss results on synthetic linearly separable datasets are outside the benchmark conditions named by the versions and are not rows. The CIFAR-10 training-error statement is aggregate; no per-model training-error values are stated.
record.test_reason: The study reports its own near-zero training classification error for CNNs trained with SGD on standard CIFAR-10 and a new NAD-flipped representation, bearing on V1 in this architectural-bias setting.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: architectural directional bias shapes feature selection and can favor memorization despite available discriminative features. The authors qualify their findings as mainly concerning separable data, especially linearly separable tasks; extension to non-separable data remains open.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains CNNs on CIFAR-10 and altered representations to examine generalization; it does not reproduce the cited random-label memorization recipe. It reports 50 epochs of SGD with a linearly decaying learning rate, momentum, and weight decay.
record.method_sensitivity: CIFAR-10 representation (original versus flipped in the NAD basis) changes test accuracy; the text reports approximately 0% training error for both.

fits_no_version.finding: Synthetic linearly separable tasks converge more slowly when their discriminative directions align with later NADs or unfavorable Fourier directions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Alignment between discriminative features and architectural directional bias affects optimization speed.

fits_no_version.finding: NAD-flipped CIFAR-10 produces substantially worse test accuracy despite approximately zero training error.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Architectural directional bias affects generalization even when training data can be fitted.

record.peer_reviewed: 34th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2020)
record.problems: Training-error results are reported only as an aggregate approximate statement, without per-model values or uncertainty. The CIFAR-10 experiments do not test corrupted labels.
record.rows_left_out: Synthetic linearly separable dataset training-loss and convergence results (Sections 2, 4.1, D.3.1 and Figures 2, S21) are not benchmark results named by the claim versions; no rows included.

untested.parts: CIFAR-100, corrupted or random labels, explicit verification of random initialization, model-size comparisons, Adam, early stopping and comparisons among regularization recipes.
Teacher-student ReLU optimization, spurious local minima and the effect of extra student neurons.
Training degradation with depth and controlled comparisons of plain networks, identity shortcuts and special initialization.
Comparisons of initialization schemes, signal or gradient preservation, and resulting training speed or trainable depth.
Learning rates relative to stability thresholds, catapult recovery, edge-of-stability dynamics and divergence.
Controlled comparisons of training speed and learning-rate tolerance with and without batch normalization or Fixup.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source for V1. Neither reduced test accuracy nor direction-dependent convergence tests the initialization, depth, width, stability-threshold or batch-normalization comparisons named in V2–V6. The synthetic optimization results are already declared in rows_left_out.

versions.untested_parts: CIFAR-100, corrupted or random labels, SGD versus Adam comparisons, smaller models, early stopping, and regularized recipes.

relationships.condition: CNNs trained for 50 epochs with SGD on standard and NAD-flipped CIFAR-10, with weight decay.
relationships.reason: Section 4.2 explicitly reports approximately 0% training error for both representations (R1, R2), supporting the training-error outcome in these settings.
relationships.display_finding: Both input representations yielded approximately 0% training error after 50 epochs.
